Kilka tygodni temu zaproponowaliśmy drobne zmiany UX w aplikacji mObywatel, które przekonują do zastrzeżenia PESELu. Nie sądziliśmy, że temat tak szybko okaże się bardzo pilny 😞 [ENG below]

Potężny wyciek danych medycznych sprzed kilku dni wstrząsnął całą Polską. Warto pamiętać, że przed konsekwencjami takich ataków można się bronić – wystarczy kilka prostych kroków w mObywatelu.

Ponieważ użytkownicy rzadko korzystają z funkcji zastrzeżenia PESELu, postanowiliśmy coś z tym zrobić – wyjść z propozycją, jak można rozwiązać problem.

Zmiany zaproponowane przez Mateusz Jankowski i Marcin Rzymek:

1. Ostrzeżenie już na głównym widoku

2. Funkcja "Zastrzeż PESEL" domyślnie w Ulubionych

3. Czytelne zaadresowanie obaw użytkowników

4. Wykorzystanie istniejącego systemu powiadomień PUSH do edukowania na temat zagrożeń

5. Nowa funkcja: "Moja Rodzina" czyli możliwość dodawania członków rodziny do swojej aplikacji i zastrzegania ich numeru PESEL

Na ten moment projekt zmian pozostaje w sferze propozycji.

Zachęcamy: Zastrzeż swój numer PESEL dzisiaj ‼️ 
_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _

A few weeks ago, we proposed some minor UX changes to the mObywatel app designed to encourage users to flag their PESEL number as restricted. We didn't expect this issue to become so urgent so quickly.

A massive medical data breach a few days ago has shaken all of Poland. It is worth remembering that you can protect yourself against the consequences of such attacks – it takes just a few simple steps in the mObywatel app.

Since users rarely utilize the PESEL restriction feature, we decided to take action and propose a solution to the problem.

Changes proposed by Mateusz Jankowski and Marcin Rzymek:

1. A warning displayed right on the main screen

2. "Restrict PESEL" feature included in "Favorites" by default

3. Clearly addressing user concerns

4. Using the existing push notification system to educate users about threats

5. New feature: "My Family" – the ability to add family members to your app and restrict their PESEL numbers

For now, the proposed changes remain just that – a proposal.

We encourage you to restrict your PESEL number today.

posts.content:
"The learning is where the value is, NOT in the artifact" ❌ We love everything about the 'Next in Commerce' episode with Eric Ries 💚 Interview PACKED with insights that might change your perspective.

1. Lean Startup was always about long-term thinking. The MVP only makes sense in service of a long-term vision – without a big goal, you'd just build the minimum product and cash out, no "learning" required

2. The real point of a startup is learning, not artifacts. AI tools risk making people mistake fast generated code for progress. Founders who outsource learning to AI (rather than sharpening their own judgment) end up with work that looks good to them but poor to everyone else

3. Don't predict the AI future – find actions robust across all scenarios. Rather than betting on utopia or doomsday, look for moves that hold up either way: understanding the technology deeply, pushing for policy disclosure, making your org "legible" to AI

4. Mission protections must be built early – "it's always too early until it's too late." Founders are told at every stage (incorporation, fundraising, IPO) that it's premature, until it's suddenly impossible. Eric blames "financial gravity" – advisors pushing conventional practices because their incentives reward transaction volume, not mission longevity

5. Durable companies share three traits, built through concrete steps. Trustworthy firms (Costco, Novo Nordisk, Anthropic) act consistently on values tied to human flourishing and can resist outside pressure. Practical steps: write the mission into the corporate charter (e.g., file as a PBC), add a "director's oath," and consider employee/foundation ownership for built-in checks and balances

posts.content:
Who can influence a purchase decision better than your old (not so old) friend, ChatGPT?

And now that trusted friend is getting ads. 🤔

ChatGPT Ads will expand to 31 European countries, including Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Austria. No keywords this time. Advertisers bid through context signals: the system reads the conversation, the landing page, and the ad copy, then decides where an ad belongs.

For e-commerce, that's an opportunity. People already ask ChatGPT what to buy, not just what exists. That's the exact moment paid placement can work.

It also raises some serious questions.

1️⃣ Trust in the recommendation. When someone asks ChatGPT what to buy, it may no longer be clear whether the answer is advice or a paid placement. 

2️⃣ No visibility into why an ad showed. Keywords used to tell advertisers exactly what they were bidding on. Context signals replace that with a black box, so nobody outside OpenAI can see the logic behind a placement.

3️⃣ GEO and paid ads might help each other, or cancel each other out. A brand with strong organic visibility in ChatGPT could end up paying for a slot it already had for free.

4️⃣ Personalization here runs on conversations, not cookies. People tell ChatGPT things they'd never type into a search bar, so feeding that into ad targeting is a different level of sensitivity than retargeting ever was.

5️⃣ Clean data is becoming the new bidding floor. This system rewards structured feeds and strong content over raw budget, which means smaller retailers without the resources to fix their data risk staying invisible no matter what they're willing to spend.

6️⃣ Attribution here has a specific gap. OpenAI's own conversion measurement is still immature, even in the US, where it launched as a manually configured service, not a self-serve one. And since the conversation stays private, advertisers can't tell whether a purchase followed the paid placement or an unpaid mention in the same reply.

So what's your read: will this make ChatGPT a better tool for buying decisions, or a harder one to trust? 

Poster made by Dominika Mielecka 💚

Engineers don’t hate Figma. They hate poorly made design systems. 😬

If every design handoff turns into a chaotic mess of endless questions, delays, and frustration, you’re likely making one of these 3 mistakes:

1️⃣ Creating 10 components when you need 1
In Figma, duplicating a component takes seconds. In code, it wastes hours. The best systems don't add more components—they make existing ones more flexible (like a single card that handles alerts, toasts, and notifications). 

2️⃣ Skipping component states
Hover, focus, disabled, loading, empty. If you don't design them, your engineers have to guess. And every guess they make is a design decision you failed to provide. 

3️⃣ Handing off pictures instead of documentation
A component isn't just a static visual. It’s behavior, interaction, and animation.
In our latest video, we break down exactly how to fix your handoff and bridge the gap between design and dev.

Stop rebuilding the wheel and start using a system built for scale.

posts.content:
You'd think RAG means more accuracy. Nope. ❌

A new Nature Medicine* study explains why. Researchers tested specialized, RAG-based clinical tools against general models like GPT and Gemini. The specialized tools were built for the job. They still lost. Those RAG-based tools landed around 88 to 90% on a medical exam, roughly 1 in 10 answers off, even with a knowledge base attached.

A knowledge base doesn't make a chatbot accurate. The study found RAG can underperform a plain general model when the data is messy or the retrieval is sloppy.

The accuracy lives in the prep. Clean, unified content. Engineered retrieval. A model that rewrites verified material instead of inventing it.

That's how we built ITI Concierge for the International Team for Implantology. Same RAG architecture the study tested. The difference was discipline.

Result: 98% of its answers were correct, relevant, and complete.✅

So the question isn't "does it use RAG." It's "who prepared the data, and how well."😎

posts.content:
98% of its answers were correct, relevant, and complete. 😮

That's the accuracy we measured for ITI Concierge, the educational chatbot for implant dentistry we built with the International Team for Implantology.

A Nature Medicine* study published this month makes that number more interesting than it looks.

Researchers tested specialized, RAG-based clinical AI tools against general-purpose models like GPT, Gemini, and Claude. The purpose-built tools were supposed to win. They didn't. Those RAG-based tools landed around 88 to 90% on a medical exam, behind every general model. ❌

The authors point to why. Adding a knowledge base to a model doesn't guarantee accuracy. When retrieval pulls the wrong material, or the model integrates it poorly, RAG drags performance down instead of up.

Their conclusion: on narrow, specialized work, the edge comes from curated retrieval and human-in-the-loop quality. Not from bolting a database onto a model.

That's the exact bet we made with ITI Concierge.

We didn't just add RAG. We rebuilt ITI's content into a clean, unified library. We engineered how the system retrieves and how it answers. The model rewrites well-prepared content, so it never has to invent anything.
RAG didn't make it accurate. The data prep did.

In implant dentistry, "roughly right" isn't an option. Accuracy here isn't a feature. That's the whole point.

Read the full story 👉 https://hubs.ly/Q04mPlBM0

*Source: Vishwanath et http://al., Nature Medicine, June 2026

Most AI conversations in large companies miss the point. Rodrigo Álvarez Bandrés from Siemens Gamesa will soon break down how one of the world's largest wind energy companies actually approaches AI adoption.

Three things every founder should hear:

1️⃣ The barriers aren't technical – they're human

Resistance to change, constant firefighting, and underdeveloped workforce skills. These are what slow AI adoption down. If you're not treating this as a change management problem first, you're solving the wrong thing.

2️⃣ Process first, then automation

Don't chase automation for its own sake. Map your end-to-end processes, find the repetitive steps that are genuine friction points, and only then introduce AI. Rodrigo's team layered it: structure your data > accelerate decision-making > automate execution. In that order.

3️⃣ Human judgment stays in the loop

The steps in any process that require real critical thinking? Those stay human.

Not because the technology isn't impressive, but because the nuance required simply isn't capturable yet. The goal is to free your people from the noise so they can spend more time on the decisions that actually matter.
